subject: Climate & Environment
title: Megafauna Collapse
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Megafauna Collapse.

hook.text: Woolly mammoths, giant sloths, and saber-toothed cats all vanished within a few thousand years.

buildup.text: Between 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, nearly all large land animals outside Africa disappeared.

discovery.text: Wherever humans arrived — Australia, the Americas, islands — megafauna vanished shortly after.

twist.text: Climate change played a role, but the timing matches human arrival too closely to ignore.

climax.text: Africa kept its megafauna because animals there evolved alongside humans over millions of years.

punchline.text: Animals that never met humans didn't survive the introduction.

quiz.question: Why did Africa retain more megafauna than other continents?
options: Animals co-evolved with humans over millions of years
African animals were larger and stronger

details.summary: Most of Earth's large animals disappeared during the late Pleistocene as humans spread across continents. Mammoths, giant sloths, saber-toothed cats, and dozens of other megafauna went extinct within thousands of years of human arrival on each continent.
details.whyItMatters: Megafauna collapse shows that human impact on biodiversity is not new — it began with our earliest migrations. Modern large-animal declines continue the same pattern.
takeaways: Roughly 80 percent of large mammals vanished in the late Pleistocene
Extinctions closely followed human arrival on each continent
Climate change and overhunting likely acted together

faq.question: Did humans or climate change cause the megafauna extinction?
faq.answer: Evidence increasingly supports a synergistic model where human hunting pressure combined with climate-driven habitat changes to push megafauna past survival thresholds. Continents that humans reached last lost megafauna last.

faq.question: Why did Africa retain more large animals than other continents?
faq.answer: African megafauna co-evolved with hominins over millions of years, developing fear and avoidance behaviors. On other continents, animals encountering humans for the first time had no instinctive defenses against this new predator.
